stem: A 25 year old lady came to the clinic with history can of headache and visual changes with bilateral milky nipple discharge what is the best next investigation that needs to be done for the patient
srcNote: No answer key is stated in the source. Incomplete choice set: only three options are provided in the source. The phrase "not sure" follows option C; no answer is explicitly marked.
expl: Headache, visual-field changes and bilateral galactorrhoea suggest a prolactinoma → check serum prolactin (and TSH, since hypothyroidism raises prolactin), then pituitary MRI.

why.A: Not the cause of bilateral milky discharge.
why.C: MRI pituitary comes after the hormone tests.

stem: A 55 years old man presented with headache, nausea and vomiting. His past medical history is significant for lung squamous cell carcinoma which was treated with surgery and chemoradiation one year ago. His vital signs are normal. He’s fully awake. His physical examination showed left upper limb weakness, what is the most likely dx?

opts.t: Obtain CT of the head which will show left parietal lesion
Obtain MRI of brain which will show right frontal lesion
Refer for thoracic, for a possible surgery

srcNote: (Management of intracranial tumors) Source note (Final 439 F Q1): pet scan doesn’t show brain Mets so we choose brain mri
expl: A treated lung cancer patient with headache, vomiting (raised ICP) and new focal weakness = brain metastasis until proven otherwise. MRI is the definitive study, and left upper-limb weakness localizes to the RIGHT (contralateral) frontal motor cortex.

why.A: Local (lung) recurrence doesn't explain raised ICP and focal weakness.
why.B: A left-sided lesion would cause right-sided weakness.
why.D: The problem is intracranial; a thoracic referral misses the brain lesion.

stem: 6 years old boy with persistent headache, vomiting and frequent falls, MRI shows midline posterior fossa tumor. What is the most likely differential diagnosis?
srcNote: (Localization of lesion within CNs) (Management of intracranial tumors) Incomplete choice set: only two options are provided in the source.
expl: The classic paediatric posterior fossa (midline/fourth ventricle) tumours are medulloblastoma, ependymoma and (pilocytic) astrocytoma.

why.B: Craniopharyngioma is suprasellar, meningioma is mainly adult, and ganglioneuroma isn't a posterior fossa tumour.

stem: A 50 years old man presented with a history of worsening early morning headache associated with nausea and progressive left sided hemiparesis for 2 months. CT was done and showed right intra-axial frontal lobe tumour surrounded by massive brain edema. Which one of the following management steps is recommended?
expl: Tumour-related (vasogenic) oedema responds to corticosteroids — dexamethasone reduces the oedema and the symptoms of raised ICP.

why.A: Duraplasty is part of decompressive surgery, not the first step for tumour oedema.
why.B: Barbiturate coma is a last-resort measure for refractory ICP.
why.D: Hyperventilation is only a brief bridge in impending herniation; it doesn't treat the oedema.

stem: What are the most common tumours in the central nervous system?
srcNote: (the most common primary brain tumors in order: 1- Meningioma 2- Glioblastoma 3- Tumors of the pituitary 4- Nerve sheath tumors (schwannoma).| (Management of intracranial tumors) Incomplete choice set: options C and D are blank in the source.
expl: The commonest CNS tumours are meningioma, glioblastoma, pituitary adenoma and nerve-sheath tumours (schwannoma).

why.A: Pilocytic astrocytoma is common in children but not among the commonest CNS tumours overall.

stem: Pt with left brain tumor has decrease level of consciousness, he presented to the ER and collapsed, his ICP was high, which of the following represent the relationship of the volume and pressure in this pt?

opts.t: There is no relation between pressure and volume
Pressure and volume diagram will shift to the right
Pressure and volume diagram will shift to the left
There is direct correlation between pressure and volume

expl: Keyed "shift to the right": ICP rises exponentially with volume (Monro–Kellie). Once compensation (CSF and venous blood displacement) is used up, the patient moves to the right onto the steep part of the curve, where a small added volume causes a large rise in ICP.

why.A: Pressure and volume are closely related.
why.C: The source keyed "right" for the decompensated position on the curve.
why.D: The relationship is exponential (flat, then steep), not a direct linear correlation.

stem: A35-year-old lady presented with visual deterioration over 3 months. She had disturbed menstrual cycle. No neurological compromise was detected in her limb examination MRI brain revealed a pituitary adenoma compressing on the optic chiasm. Which of the following visual field deficits likely results from this lesion?
expl: A pituitary adenoma compresses the optic chiasm from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres → bitemporal hemianopia (with hormonal disturbance, e.g. menstrual irregularity).

why.A: A homonymous quadrantanopia comes from the optic radiations (temporal or parietal).
why.B: A homonymous hemianopia comes from the optic tract, radiations or occipital cortex.
why.C: A central scotoma comes from optic-nerve/macular disease.

stem: Brain MRI showing intra-axial heterogenous enhancing lesion in the right premotor gyrus.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A single intra-axial, heterogeneously enhancing lesion within the brain parenchyma (premotor gyrus) → high-grade primary brain tumour (e.g. glioblastoma).

why.A: Metastases are classically multiple, well-circumscribed and at the grey–white junction.
why.B: Lymphoma is usually periventricular and homogeneously enhancing.
why.D: An abscess is a smooth ring-enhancing lesion with restricted diffusion, usually with an infective history.

stem: A 20 y/o man presented with seizure and on CT scan there is an enhancing lesion of left inferior frontal lobe. What is the abnormality?
expl: The left inferior frontal gyrus is Broca's area (dominant hemisphere) → expressive (motor) aphasia: difficulty in expression with relatively preserved comprehension.

why.C: Impaired articulation is dysarthria (motor speech), not a language defect.

stem: What is the most potent and fastest way to reduce the intracranial pressure?
expl: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ → cerebral vasoconstriction → rapid fall in ICP within minutes — the fastest measure (used briefly as a bridge, PCO₂ 30–35).

stem: A 60 years old man presented with progressive left sided weakness, more apparent in upper extremity over the last 3 months. He is afebrile and his cranial nerves examination showed left upper motor neuron facial nerve palsy. He is oriented with normal speech. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Progressive (over months) left-sided weakness, arm > leg, with a left UMN facial palsy in a 60-year-old points to a growing right frontal mass — glioblastoma is the commonest malignant primary tumour at this age.

why.A: A stroke is sudden, not progressive over 3 months.
why.C: A cerebellar tumour causes ataxia, not hemiparesis with UMN facial palsy.
why.D: A left-sided lesion would cause right-sided weakness.

stem: Early morning headache is a sign of increased intracranial pressure. What is the mechanism underlying this headache?
expl: During sleep, ventilation falls → PaCO₂ rises → cerebral vasodilation → more intracranial blood volume → ICP rises further in a patient with reduced compliance → early-morning headache (with vomiting).

stem: 10 years old girl presented with headache and instability of her gait. Physical examination was significant for past-pointing and pendular reflexes. These findings are most likely to occur with which one of the following?
expl: Headache (raised ICP) with cerebellar signs — past-pointing (dysmetria) and pendular reflexes — in a child → cerebellar medulloblastoma.

why.B: ALS is an adult motor-neurone disease with mixed UMN/LMN signs, not cerebellar signs.
why.C: Meningomyelocele is a congenital spinal defect present from birth.
why.D: Syringomyelia gives cape-like dissociated sensory loss.

stem: Which of the following constitutes Cushing’s triad?

opts.t: High systolic, low HR, low RR
Low systolic, high HR, low RR
High systolic, low HR, high RR
Low systolic, low HR, low RR

srcNote: physiological nervous system response to acute elevations of intracranial pressure (ICP), resulting in the Cushing triad of widened pulse pressure (increasing systolic, decreasing diastolic) bradycardia, and irregular respirations.
expl: Cushing's triad of raised ICP: hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular/slow respiration.

stem: Which of the following studies should be primarily performed if a brain tumor is suspected?
expl: CT is fast and widely available and is the first study when a brain tumour is suspected (especially acutely); MRI then characterizes it.

why.D: Transcranial Doppler measures intracranial blood flow.

stem: Treatment of raised intracranial pressure includes which one of the following?

opts.t: Elevation of the foot end of the bed

expl: Head elevation (~30°) improves venous drainage and lowers ICP.
